claim: Mutations in the human PURA gene cause the neurodevelopmental PURA syndrome.
source: Mutations in the human PURA gene cause the neurodevelopmental PURA syndrome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Almost all reported mutations in PURA result in full disease penetrance.
source: In contrast to several other monogenetic disorders, almost all reported mutations in this nucleic acid-binding protein result in the full disease penetrance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the introduction and discussion sections.

claim: Patient mutations across PURA impair its co-localization with processing bodies.
source: In this study, we observed that patient mutations across PURA impair its previously reported co-localization with processing bodies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Patient mutations in PURA either destroyed the folding integrity, RNA binding, or dimerization of PURA.
source: These mutations either destroyed the folding integrity, RNA binding, or dimerization of PURA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental results including CD spectroscopy, EMSA, and NanoBRET assays.

claim: The crystal structures of the N- and C-terminal PUR domains of human PURA were solved.
source: We also solved the crystal structures of the N- and C-terminal PUR domains of human PURA and combined them with molecular dynamics simulations and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and detailed in the Results section with PDB IDs provided.

claim: PURA exhibits unusually high dynamics and structural promiscuity.
source: The observed unusually high dynamics and structural promiscuity of PURA indicated that this protein is particularly susceptible to mutations impairing its structural integrity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by crystal structure analysis, NMR data, and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The structural promiscuity of PURA explains why even conservative mutations result in full penetrance of symptoms in PURA syndrome patients.
source: It offers an explanation why even conservative mutations across PURA result in the full penetrance of symptoms in patients with PURA syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed extensively in the Discussion section based on structural and functional data.

claim: PURA is ubiquitously expressed.
source: It is ubiquitously expressed and has been implicated in several cellular processes, including transcriptional and translational gene regulation as well as mRNA transport in neurons (Chepenik et al., 1998; Gallia et al., 2001; Haas et al., 1993; Haas et al., 1995; Johnson et al., 2006; Kobayashi et al., 2000; Mitsumori et al., 2017; Tretiakova et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: PURA has been implicated in transcriptional and translational gene regulation as well as mRNA transport in neurons.
source: It is ubiquitously expressed and has been implicated in several cellular processes, including transcriptional and translational gene regulation as well as mRNA transport in neurons (Chepenik et al., 1998; Gallia et al., 2001; Haas et al., 1993; Haas et al., 1995; Johnson et al., 2006; Kobayashi et al., 2000; Mitsumori et al., 2017; Tretiakova et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: PURA is important for postnatal brain development.
source: Results from two independent knock-out mouse models demonstrated that PURA is important for postnatal brain development (Hokkanen et al., 2012; Khalili et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to two independent mouse studies.

claim: PURA has been implicated as a modulator of neurodegenerative disorders such as FXTAS and ALS-FTD.
source: Accordingly, PURA has been implicated as a modulator of neurodegenerative disorders, such as fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), and the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) frontotemporal dementia spectrum disorder (Swinnen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: PURA is present in pathological RNA foci of FXTAS and ALS-FTD.
source: PURA was reported to be present in the pathological RNA foci of both disorders and to protect against RNA toxicity upon ectopic overexpression (Mori et al., 2013; Rossi et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2018; Swinnen et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: PURA co-localizes with an ALS-causing variant of FUS protein in stress granules of ALS patients.
source: In addition, PURA was shown to co-localize with an ALS-causing variant of the FUS protein in stress granules of ALS patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation.

claim: Overexpression of PURA reduced the toxicity of mutant FUS by preventing its mis-localization.
source: Importantly, overexpression of PURA reduced the toxicity of mutant FUS by preventing its mis-localization (Daigle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: In 2014, two studies reported that PURA syndrome is caused by sporadic mutations in the PURA gene.
source: In 2014, two studies reported that a monogenetic neurodevelopmental disorder is caused by sporadic mutations in the PURA gene (Hunt et al., 2014; Lalani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with two supporting citations.

claim: Hallmarks of PURA syndrome include developmental delay, moderate to severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, epileptic seizures, and feeding difficulties.
source: Hallmarks of this so-called PURA syndrome are developmental delay, moderate to severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, epileptic seizures, and feeding difficulties, among others (Reijnders et al., 2018; Johannesen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Three conserved sequence regions termed PUR repeats I, II, and III fold into globular domains.
source: Based on the crystal structures of PURA from Drosophila melanogaster (dmPURA), three conserved sequence regions termed PUR repeats I, II, and III were identified to fold into globular domains (Graebsch et al., 2010; Graebsch et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations to crystal structure studies.

claim: PUR repeat I and II assemble into an N-terminal PUR domain via intramolecular interactions.
source: Whereas PUR repeat I and II assemble into an N-terminal PUR domain via intramolecular interactions, two C-terminal PUR repeats III from different molecules interact with each other and thus mediate dimerization of PURA.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on previous structural studies.

claim: Two C-terminal PUR repeats III from different molecules interact with each other and mediate dimerization of PURA.
source: Whereas PUR repeat I and II assemble into an N-terminal PUR domain via intramolecular interactions, two C-terminal PUR repeats III from different molecules interact with each other and thus mediate dimerization of PURA.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction based on previous structural studies.

claim: All PUR domains belong to the class of the PC4-like protein family.
source: All these PUR domains belong to the class of the PC4-like protein family, which mainly bind single-stranded nucleic acids and can unwind double-stranded DNA and RNA (Janowski and Niessing, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: PC4-like proteins mainly bind single-stranded nucleic acids and can unwind double-stranded DNA and RNA.
source: All these PUR domains belong to the class of the PC4-like protein family, which mainly bind single-stranded nucleic acids and can unwind double-stranded DNA and RNA (Janowski and Niessing, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Both PUR domains possess the typical PC4-like β-β-β-β-α-(linker)-β-β-β-β-α topology.
source: Although both PUR domains possess the typical PC4-like β-β-β-β-α-(linker)-β-β-β-β-α topology, the N-terminal domain has been suggested to be the main RNA/DNA interaction entity (Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The N-terminal PUR domain has been suggested to be the main RNA/DNA interaction entity.
source: Although both PUR domains possess the typical PC4-like β-β-β-β-α-(linker)-β-β-β-β-α topology, the N-terminal domain has been suggested to be the main RNA/DNA interaction entity (Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Homology models based on dmPURA crystal structures were used to predict effects of PURA syndrome-causing mutations on human PURA structural integrity.
source: In a previous study, homology models based on the dmPURA crystal structures (Graebsch et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2016) were used to predict in silico the effects of PURA syndrome-causing mutations on the structural integrity of the human PURA protein (Reijnders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mutations in PURA could be classified into groups that likely either do or do not impair structural integrity, but these predictions remained speculative.
source: While these mutations could be classified into groups that likely either do or do not impair the structural integrity of PURA, these predictions remained speculative (Reijnders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: No hot-spot regions could be identified in the PURA protein sequence that trigger PURA syndrome.
source: Surprisingly, in contrast to phenotypically related genetic diseases such as the Rett syndrome (Lombardi et al., 2015), no hot-spot regions could be identified in the protein sequence that trigger the PURA syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to a related disorder for comparison.

claim: Almost all mutations across the PURA protein sequence appear to result in the full disease spectrum.
source: With the exception of the unstructured N-terminal region and the very C-terminus, almost all mutations across the protein sequence appear to result in the full disease spectrum (Johannesen et al., 2021; Reijnders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There is an underrepresentation of mild phenotypes in patients with PURA syndrome.
source: To date, we fail to understand why there is such an underrepresentation of mild phenotypes in patients with PURA syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a key question motivating the study.

claim: More than 270 different pathogenic variants in the PURA gene have been identified in over 650 patients with confirmed PURA syndrome.
source: Currently, more than 270 different pathogenic variants in the PURA gene have been identified in over 650 patients with confirmed PURA syndrome (personal communication: PURA Foundation Australia).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to personal communication.

claim: Wild-type hsPURA co-localizes to stress granules in HeLa cells.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Daigle et al., 2016; Markmiller et al., 2018), we observed that hsPURA co-localizes to stress granules in HeLa cells (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Patient-related variants K97E, I206F, and F233del of hsPURA do not show significant changes in association to stress granules.
source: As we did not observe significant changes in the association of patient-related variants of hsPURA to stress granules, it is suggested that this feature may not constitute a major hallmark of the PURA syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The nucleic acid-binding-deficient mutant hsPURA m11 failed to co-localize to G3BP1-positive stress granules.
source: In contrast, the nucleic acid-binding-deficient mutant hsPURA m11 failed to co-localize to G3BP1-positive granules, indicating that RNA binding by hsPURA is necessary for its co-localization with stress granules.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B, C.

claim: RNA binding by hsPURA is necessary for its co-localization with stress granules.
source: In contrast, the nucleic acid-binding-deficient mutant hsPURA m11 failed to co-localize to G3BP1-positive granules, indicating that RNA binding by hsPURA is necessary for its co-localization with stress granules.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1B, C.

claim: PURA knockdown resulted in reduced sizes of stress granules.
source: A PURA knockdown did not alter the total number of microscopically visible stress granules but resulted in a greater ratio of smaller stress granules (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: PURA knockdown did not alter the total number of microscopically visible stress granules.
source: A PURA knockdown did not alter the total number of microscopically visible stress granules but resulted in a greater ratio of smaller stress granules (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: PURA is not essential for stress-granule formation.
source: Although this finding suggests that PURA is not essential for stress-granule formation, it should be noted that the knockdown did not completely eliminate PURA levels and hence a stronger effect on stress granules could occur in a complete knock-out of PURA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the knockdown experiment data.

claim: Endogenous hsPURA co-localized with G3BP1 upon stress treatment with arsenite.
source: As expected, endogenous hsPURA co-localized with G3BP1 upon stress treatment with 500 µM arsenite PURA (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B) and thus behaved similar to overexpressed hsPURA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: Overexpressed hsPURA co-localizes with the P-body marker DCP1A in HeLa cells.
source: Co-staining with the marker DCP1A indeed confirmed a co-localization of overexpressed hsPURA in P-bodies of HeLa cells (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The PURA m11 mutant failed to accumulate in P-bodies.
source: As for stress granules, the PURA m11 mutant failed to accumulate in P-bodies, indicating that RNA binding of PURA contributes to its P-body localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A, B.

claim: RNA binding of PURA contributes to its P-body localization.
source: As for stress granules, the PURA m11 mutant failed to accumulate in P-bodies, indicating that RNA binding of PURA contributes to its P-body localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2A, B.

claim: The patient-related genetic variants K97E and F233del of hsPURA showed significantly reduced co-localization to P-bodies.
source: In addition, the patient-related genetic variants K97E and F233del of hsPURA showed significantly reduced co-localization to P-bodies (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: The majority of tested patient variations result in impaired P-body localization.
source: In summary, these experiments indicate that P-body localization of hsPURA requires its RNA-binding activity, and that the majority of tested patient variations result in impaired P-body localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the P-body localization experiments.

claim: Dimerization is important for PURA's P-body association.
source: Furthermore, since F233del has been predicted to have impaired dimerization properties (Reijnders et al., 2018), these findings suggest dimerization to be important for PURA's P-body association.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the P-body localization data and previous predictions.

claim: hsPURA does not readily phase separate with total cellular RNA under the tested experimental conditions.
source: In contrast to this control, no indication of phase separation was observed for hsPURA either in the presence or absence of total HeLa cell RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phase separation assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: It seems unlikely that P-body formation directly depends on phase separation by hsPURA.
source: Of note, this observation does not exclude the possibility that hsPURA can undergo phase separation under different experimental conditions, for instance in presence of additional co-factors. However, when putting this observation in perspective with previous reports, it seems unlikely that P-body formation directly depends on phase separation by hsPURA, but rather on its recently reported function as gene regulator of the essential P-body core factors LSM14a and DDX6 (Molitor et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the phase separation data and previous reports.

claim: Recombinantly expressed hsPURA fragments with mutations R199P and I206F could not be purified due to protein insolubility.
source: Even after extensive optimization, recombinantly expressed hsPURA fragments with the mutations R199P and I206F (full-length variant and N-terminal PUR domain consisting of repeats I–II; PURA I–II) as well as F233del and R245P (full-length variant and C-terminal PUR domain consisting of two repeats III; PURA III) could not be purified due to protein insolubility (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and documented in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Recombinantly expressed hsPURA fragments with mutations F233del and R245P could not be purified due to protein insolubility.
source: Even after extensive optimization, recombinantly expressed hsPURA fragments with the mutations R199P and I206F (full-length variant and N-terminal PUR domain consisting of repeats I–II; PURA I–II) as well as F233del and R245P (full-length variant and C-terminal PUR domain consisting of two repeats III; PURA III) could not be purified due to protein insolubility (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and documented in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: N-terminal PUR domains (PURA I–II) with mutations K97E and R140P were soluble and could be purified to near homogeneity.
source: In contrast, N-terminal PUR domains (PURA I–II) with either of the two remaining mutations K97E and R140P were soluble and could be purified to near homogeneity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on recombinant expression experiments.

claim: The crystal structure of hsPURA III was determined at 1.7 Å resolution.
source: Since Drosophila and human PURA have a rather moderate sequence identity of 46%, we decided to establish a better experimental basis for predicting the structural effects of patient-derived genetic variations and determined the crystal structure of the fragment P215-K280 (i.e. hsPURA III) at 1.7 Å resolution (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and the structure is shown in Figure 3A with crystallographic data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The C-terminal PUR domain of hsPURA possesses the typical four antiparallel β-strands and one α-helix.
source: The structure of the C-terminal PUR-domain possesses the typical four antiparallel β-strands and one α-helix.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the crystal structure analysis.

claim: The C-terminal PUR domain of hsPURA is built from two PUR repeats III of independent protein chains that interact with each other to form an intermolecular homodimer.
source: Like in the previously published dmPURA III structure (Weber et al., 2016), the C-terminal PUR domain of hsPURA is built from two PUR repeats III of independent protein chains that interact with each other to form an intermolecular homodimer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the crystal structure analysis.

claim: The hsPURA III dimer shows high structural similarity to dmPURA III with r.m.s.d. of 1.26 Å for 125 superimposed Cα atoms and 50% sequence identity.
source: The hsPURA III dimer shows high structural similarity to dmPURA III with root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 1.26 Å for 125 superimposed Cα atoms and 50% of sequence identity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The C-terminal PUR domain (hsPURA III) is able to interact with nucleic acids.
source: When performing gel electrophoresis mobility shift assays (EMSAs) we indeed observed RNA binding (Figure 3B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EMSA data in Figure 3B, C.

claim: PURA can separate double-stranded nucleic acids in an ATP-independent fashion.
source: It had been previously reported that PURA can separate double-stranded (ds) nucleic acids in an ATP-independent fashion (Darbinian et al., 2001; Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: The hsPURA III fragment shows strand separation activity.
source: We indeed observed strand separation in presence of the hsPURA III fragment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by unwinding assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: RNA binding and dsDNA strand separation by full-length hsPURA was much more efficient than by the PUR III domain.
source: Of note, RNA binding as well as dsDNA strand separation by full-length hsPURA was much more efficient than by the PUR III domain (Figure 3D, E), indicating potential cooperativity of the N- and C-terminal PUR domains in unwinding double-stranded nucleic acids.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 3D, E.

claim: There is potential cooperativity of the N- and C-terminal PUR domains in unwinding double-stranded nucleic acids.
source: Of note, RNA binding as well as dsDNA strand separation by full-length hsPURA was much more efficient than by the PUR III domain (Figure 3D, E), indicating potential cooperativity of the N- and C-terminal PUR domains in unwinding double-stranded nucleic acids.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of full-length and domain fragment activities.

claim: The F233del mutation is predicted to impair the structural integrity of the C-terminal hsPURA dimerization domain.
source: While failure to obtain soluble recombinant PURA with F233del prevented a direct biophysical assessment of its dimerization state in vitro (Supplementary file 1a), this observation already indicated a misfolding of the C-terminal PUR domain upon mutation. Consistent with this observation is also the interpretation from homology modeling based on the previously published dmPURA III structure (Reijnders et al., 2018). There, the mutation was predicted to impair the structural integrity of the C-terminal hsPURA dimerization domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on insolubility data and previous homology modeling.

claim: F233 is part of the β-sheet and interacts with the α-helix of the other PUR repeat III within the PUR domain, contributing to dimerization.
source: F233 is part of the β-sheet and interacts with the α-helix of the other PUR repeat III within the PUR domain, contributing to dimerization (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: In the PURA F233del variant, deletion of one residue results in opposite orientation of all subsequent amino acids in the β-strand, likely resulting in fold disruption of the β-sheet and possibly impaired dimerization.
source: Since in the PURA F233del variant, one residue is deleted, the orientation of all subsequent amino acids in the β-strand adopt the opposite orientation, likely resulting in a fold disruption of the β-sheet and possibly in impaired dimerization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: The R245P mutation likely impairs β-strand folding by introducing a kink, which could impact dimerization.
source: In the case of the R245P variant (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), the exchange into proline also likely impairs β-strand folding by introducing a kink, which could also impact dimerization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: hsPURA bearing the F233del and R245P patient variants showed strongly reduced dimerization signal intensities in NanoBRET assays.
source: While for hsPURA I–III the signal intensities above the background level clearly indicated dimerization (Figure 3F), protein fragments with either the F233del or the R245P variant showed strongly reduced signal intensities. This observation implies impairment of PURA dimerization in patients bearing either of these heterozygous variants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by NanoBRET data in Figure 3F.

claim: F233del and R245P mutations impair PURA dimerization in patients bearing these heterozygous variants.
source: While for hsPURA I–III the signal intensities above the background level clearly indicated dimerization (Figure 3F), protein fragments with either the F233del or the R245P variant showed strongly reduced signal intensities. This observation implies impairment of PURA dimerization in patients bearing either of these heterozygous variants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on NanoBRET data.

claim: The crystal structure of hsPURA I–II was determined.
source: For a better understanding of the structural impact of genetic variations in the N-terminal PUR domain (hsPURA I–II), we determined its structure (fragments E57–E212) by X-ray crystallography (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and the structure is shown in Figure 4A with crystallographic data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The N-terminal PUR domain resembles the previously published PURA structure from D. melanogaster with an average r.m.s.d. of 1.2 Å.
source: The N-terminal PUR domain resembles the previously published PURA structure from D. melanogaster (Graebsch et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2016) (dmPURA I–II WT) with an average r.m.s.d. of 1.2 Å (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The four molecules of hsPURA I–II within the asymmetric unit of the crystal lattice showed marked differences in loop regions and at the edges of β-sheets.
source: However, in contrast to this invertebrate structure, we observed for hsPURA I–II that the four molecules within its asymmetric unit of the crystal lattice showed marked differences in its loop regions and in particular at the edges of the β-sheets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: hsPURA I–II has greater structural flexibility than average domain folds and most likely than its D. melanogaster ortholog.
source: This suggested greater structural flexibility than average domain folds and most likely than its D. melanogaster ortholog.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the crystal structure analysis showing differences between molecules in the asymmetric unit.

claim: hsPURA I–II quantitatively bound a 24-mer CGG-repeat RNA.
source: While hsPURA I–II quantitatively bound a 24-mer CGG-repeat RNA, the hsPURA I–II K97E-variant protein showed moderately but significantly decreased RNA binding (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EMSA data in Figure 4C, D.

claim: The hsPURA I–II K97E variant protein showed moderately but significantly decreased RNA binding.
source: While hsPURA I–II quantitatively bound a 24-mer CGG-repeat RNA, the hsPURA I–II K97E-variant protein showed moderately but significantly decreased RNA binding (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EMSA data in Figure 4C, D.

claim: Impaired RNA binding upon K97E mutation is expected due to change of surface electrostatic potential from positive to negative.
source: Impaired RNA binding upon K97E mutation is not surprising as a change of the surface electrostatic potential from positive to negative may impact its interaction with nucleic acids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: hsPURA I–II R140P did not show impaired RNA binding.
source: In contrast, hsPURA I–II R140P did not show impaired RNA binding (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EMSA data in Figure 4C, D.

claim: R140P might be a benign variant and does not have disease-causing properties.
source: This finding indicates that R140P might be a benign variant and does not have disease-causing properties.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the RNA binding data.

claim: The hsPURA I–II m11 variant showed no detectable RNA binding in EMSA.
source: As a negative control, the N-terminal PUR domain containing 11 selected point mutations was employed (hsPURA I–II m11; Figure 1—figure supplement 2). Since these mutations were introduced to abolish the interaction of hsPURA with nucleic acids, this mutated protein showed no detectable RNA binding in EMSA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by EMSA data.

claim: hsPURA I–II showed considerable strand-separating activity.
source: While hsPURA I–II showed considerable strand-separating activity in this assay, the nucleic acid-binding-deficient m11 variant expectedly failed to separate dsDNA (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by unwinding assay data in Figure 4E, F.

claim: The nucleic acid-binding-deficient m11 variant failed to separate dsDNA.
source: While hsPURA I–II showed considerable strand-separating activity in this assay, the nucleic acid-binding-deficient m11 variant expectedly failed to separate dsDNA (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by unwinding assay data in Figure 4E, F.

claim: The hsPURA I–II K97E variant showed a loss of strand-separation activity by 90%.
source: With an effect considerably stronger than observed for RNA binding (Figure 4C, D), the hsPURA I–II K97E variant showed a loss of strand-separation activity by 90% (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by unwinding assay data in Figure 4E, F.

claim: hsPURA I–II R140P variant showed wild-type-like separation of dsDNA.
source: In contrast, hsPURA I–II R140P variant showed wild-type-like separation of dsDNA (Figure 4E, F), further supporting our previous interpretation from RNA-binding analyses that the genetic variant R140P is likely functional.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by unwinding assay data in Figure 4E, F.

claim: The CD spectra for hsPURA I–II and hsPURA I–II R140P showed a typical alpha–beta profile, suggesting proper folding.
source: The spectra for both, hsPURA I–II and the hsPURA I–II R140P variant showed a typical alpha–beta profile (Figure 5A), suggesting a proper folding of the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CD spectroscopy data in Figure 5A.

claim: The CD spectrum for hsPURA I–II K97E indicated a strongly altered secondary structure content.
source: In contrast, the spectrum for hsPURA I–II K97E indicated a strongly altered secondary structure content.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CD spectroscopy data in Figure 5A.

claim: The K97E mutation affecting structural integrity was unexpected as it was predicted that this surface mutation would not affect the protein's structural integrity.
source: This observation was unexpected as we had predicted that this surface mutation would not affect the protein's structural integrity this study and Reijnders et al., 2018.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison with previous predictions.

claim: The crystal structure of hsPURA I–II K97E was solved at 2.45 Å resolution.
source: To understand how exactly the surface-exposed K97E mutation alters the domain folding of PURA (Figure 5A), we solved the crystal structure of hsPURA I–II K97E (Figure 5B–E, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and the structure is shown in Figure 5B, C with crystallographic data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the hsPURA I–II K97E crystal contained two molecules showing good overall fold similarity to hsPURA I–II.
source: The asymmetric unit of the crystal contained two molecules of hsPURA I–II K97E and showed good overall fold similarity to the hsPURA I–II structure (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B, C.

claim: The two molecules of hsPURA I–II K97E from the asymmetric unit revealed unusual differences with r.m.s.d. of 1.48 Å for 125 superimposed Cα atoms.
source: However, an overlay of both molecules of the K97E-variant protein from the asymmetric unit also revealed unusual differences between them with r.m.s.d. of 1.48 Å for 125 superimposed Cα atoms.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis.

claim: One molecule of hsPURA I–II K97E (chain A) showed a fold very similar to hsPURA I–II with average r.m.s.d. 1.09 Å.
source: While one of these molecules (chain A, Figure 5B) showed a fold very similar to hsPURA I–II (average r.m.s.d. 1.09 Å, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), the second molecule (chain B) displayed much greater structural changes (average r.m.s.d. 1.61 Å, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The second molecule of hsPURA I–II K97E (chain B) displayed much greater structural changes with average r.m.s.d. 1.61 Å.
source: While one of these molecules (chain A, Figure 5B) showed a fold very similar to hsPURA I–II (average r.m.s.d. 1.09 Å, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), the second molecule (chain B) displayed much greater structural changes (average r.m.s.d. 1.61 Å, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In chain B of hsPURA I–II K97E, a shift of register in the β-sheet by one amino acid in strand β5 and by two amino acids in strand β6 was observed.
source: These differences were especially pronounced in PUR repeat II (Figure 5D, E), where we observed a shift of register in the β-sheet by one amino acid in strand β5 (Figure 5D) and by two amino acids in strand β6 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D, E.

claim: The β-ridge appears to be structurally the most divergent part of hsPURA I–II.
source: From all the areas of the structure, the β-ridge appears to be structurally the most divergent part.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: The K97E point mutation induces unusual change in the β-sheet arrangement without destroying the domain's overall scaffold.
source: It is surprising that the K97E point mutation, which is located on the β4 strand of the β-ridge, induces the observed unusual change in the β-sheet arrangement (Figure 5C–E) without destroying the domain's overall scaffold.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: The N-terminal PUR domain has great structural flexibility and promiscuity in folding, which results in misfolding upon mutation of a surface-exposed residue.
source: Together these findings indicate great structural flexibility of the N-terminal PUR domain and promiscuity in folding, which results in misfolding upon mutation of a surface-exposed residue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the crystal structure analysis of wild-type and K97E variant.

claim: NMR measurements showed that the K97E mutation does not induce global unfolding of hsPURA I–II, but rather triggers structural rearrangements mostly in the β-strand region.
source: Together, this shows that the K97E mutation does not induce global unfolding of hsPURA I–II, but rather triggers structural rearrangements mostly in the β-strand region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on NMR data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Molecular dynamics simulations showed that hsPURA I–II K97E has higher flexibility than wild-type in several regions including the N-terminal part of the α1 helix and the C-terminal end of β5 and β6.
source: However, there are some statistically significant differences between the two proteins. The most significant differences concentrate on the two ends of the α1 helix, as well as the β5, β6, and β7 segments. In these regions, the K97E variant shows higher flexibility than the WT, with the N-terminal part of the α1 helix and the C-terminal end of β5 and β6 having the greatest gap between the two variants.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The crystal structure of hsPURA I–II R140P was solved at 2.15 Å resolution.
source: To assess if this variant has a rather local effect on the structural integrity of PURA that may not be detectable by CD spectroscopy, we solved the crystal structure of hsPURA I–II R140P at 2.15 Å resolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B with crystallographic data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: No major structural differences were visible between hsPURA I–II WT and R140P variant with average r.m.s.d. of 0.89 Å for 133 Cα atoms aligned.
source: Since no major structural differences were visible between hsPURA I–II WT and R140P variant (average r.m.s.d. of 0.89 Å for 133 Cα atoms aligned, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), we concluded that this genetic variation is unlikely to impair the structural integrity of hsPURA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The genetic variation R140P is unlikely to impair the structural integrity of hsPURA.
source: Since no major structural differences were visible between hsPURA I–II WT and R140P variant (average r.m.s.d. of 0.89 Å for 133 Cα atoms aligned, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), we concluded that this genetic variation is unlikely to impair the structural integrity of hsPURA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on structural comparison.

claim: Reduced stress-granule association of functionally impaired hsPURA variants may not be a core feature of PURA syndrome.
source: Together these findings suggest that (1) reduced stress-granule association of functionally impaired hsPURA variants may not be a core feature of the PURA syndrome and (2) impaired stress-granule formation is not very likely to be directly responsible for the etiology of this disorder.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the stress granule localization experiments.

claim: Impaired stress-granule formation is not very likely to be directly responsible for the etiology of PURA syndrome.
source: Together these findings suggest that (1) reduced stress-granule association of functionally impaired hsPURA variants may not be a core feature of the PURA syndrome and (2) impaired stress-granule formation is not very likely to be directly responsible for the etiology of this disorder.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the stress granule localization experiments.

claim: Impaired P-body association of hsPURA may play a role in the etiology of PURA syndrome.
source: In light of this report, our finding that patient-derived variants show impaired P-body association of hsPURA (Figure 2) provide further evidence for a potential role of P-body localization of hsPURA for the etiology of PURA syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the P-body localization data and previous reports.

claim: The flexibility and promiscuity of hsPURA domain folding render this protein particularly susceptible to mutations, even when amino-acid substitutions impose only moderate changes to local charge and stereochemistry.
source: Our findings suggest that the flexibility and promiscuity of hsPURA domain folding render this protein particularly susceptible to mutations, even when amino-acid substitutions impose only moderate changes to the local charge and stereochemistry.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The structural property of PUR domains might explain why so many genetic variations across the sequence of hsPURA result in the full disease spectrum.
source: This property of PUR domains might offer a structural explanation for why so many genetic variations across the sequence of hsPURA result in the full disease spectrum.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the structural findings.

claim: Neither functional in vitro experiments nor structural assessment of hsPURA I–II R140P yielded any significant differences from the wild-type protein.
source: In our assessment, neither the functional in vitro experiments nor the structural assessment of hsPURA I–II R140P yielded any significant differences from the wild-type protein (Figure 4C–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on multiple experimental results.

claim: The experimental findings are consistent with R140P being a benign variant.
source: These experimental findings are consistent with R140P being rather a benign variant.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental data.

claim: R140P is now listed in the NCBI ClinVar database as being of 'uncertain significance'.
source: Consequently, the R140P variant is now listed in the NCBI ClinVar database to be of 'uncertain significance' (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar/variation/192343/).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a reference to the ClinVar database.

claim: There is a clear correlation between defects observed in in vitro analyses and the reported pathogenicity in patients.
source: In summary, an assessment of the different genetic variations in hsPURA indicates a clear correlation between defects observed in in vitro analyses and the reported pathogenicity in patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the overall experimental findings.

claim: In vitro analyses may serve as a diagnostic tool to distinguish pathogenic from benign genetic variations in PURA.
source: Hence, in future such in vitro analyses may serve as a diagnostic tool to distinguish pathogenic from benign genetic variations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the correlation between in vitro and clinical data.

claim: For all cases where patient variants were predicted to have folding defects, expression tests with recombinant proteins resulted in insoluble samples.
source: Some of the selected patient variants of hsPURA were previously predicted to have folding defects (Reijnders et al., 2018). Of note, for all these cases expression tests with recombinant proteins resulted in insoluble samples, indicating that these variant proteins indeed have impaired folding (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on recombinant expression data.

claim: Predictions of misfolding events appear reliable for PURA variants.
source: Whereas predictions of such misfolding events appear reliable, the examples of R140P (benign) and K97E (pathogenic) indicate that structural predictions of surface-exposed residues seem more complicated.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on comparison of predictions with experimental results.

claim: Structural predictions of surface-exposed residues in PURA are more complicated.
source: Whereas predictions of such misfolding events appear reliable, the examples of R140P (benign) and K97E (pathogenic) indicate that structural predictions of surface-exposed residues seem more complicated.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the R140P and K97E examples.

claim: Moderate surface mutations such as K97E can result in promiscuous folding and the full spectrum of disease symptoms.
source: In fact, the observed great promiscuity of folding of PUR domains indicates that also moderate surface mutations such as K97E can result in promiscuous folding and the full spectrum of disease symptoms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the K97E structural and functional data.

claim: In vitro and structural studies are suitable tools to classify genetic variants in the hsPURA gene as potentially pathogenic or benign.
source: Our study may serve as proof-of-principle that in vitro and structural studies are suitable tools to classify genetic variants in the hsPURA gene as potentially pathogenic or benign.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.

claim: PURA was recently shown to be required for P-body formation in HeLa cells and fibroblasts.
source: Since hsPURA was recently shown to be required for P-body formation in HeLa cells and fibroblasts (Molitor et al., 2023), PURA-dependent liquid-phase separation could potentially also directly contribute to the formation of these granules.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: A hsPURA knockdown in HeLa and fibroblast cells resulted in down-regulation of the essential P-body proteins LSM14a and DDX6.
source: In a recent study, it was shown that a hsPURA knockdown in HeLa and in fibroblast cells resulted in down-regulation of the essential P-body proteins LSM14a and DDX6 and, most likely as a direct consequence, in strongly impaired P-body formation (Molitor et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: A hsPURA knockdown resulted in strongly impaired P-body formation, most likely as a direct consequence of down-regulation of LSM14a and DDX6.
source: In a recent study, it was shown that a hsPURA knockdown in HeLa and in fibroblast cells resulted in down-regulation of the essential P-body proteins LSM14a and DDX6 and, most likely as a direct consequence, in strongly impaired P-body formation (Molitor et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The experimentally determined structures of human N- and C-terminal PUR domains offer more physiological structural reference points for future assessments of novel hsPURA mutations.
source: We expect that our experimentally determined structures of the human N- and C-terminal PUR domains offer more physiological structural reference points for future assessments of novel hsPURA mutations and their potential pathogenicity in patients.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the study.
